overview.headline: How bills become laws and how House and Senate differ

keyPoints.point: Congress serves as lawmaking branch of federal government
keyPoints.quote: Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government.

keyPoints.point: bill passes one body of Congress then goes through similar process of research and voting in other body
keyPoints.quote: If the bill passes one body of Congress, it goes to the other body to go through a similar process of research, discussion, changes, and voting.

keyPoints.point: President can approve bill and sign into law or refuse approval through veto
keyPoints.quote: The president can approve the bill and sign it into law.

keyPoints.point: House can initiate tax legislation while Senate handles nominations
keyPoints.quote: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation

keyTerms.gloss: proposal for new law or change to existing law
keyTerms.quote: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

keyTerms.gloss: group that will research and discuss changes to bill
keyTerms.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.
Or the president can refuse to approve a bill. This is called a veto.

keyTerms.gloss: action that cannot be overridden by Congress when session ends
keyTerms.quote: This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress.
